read.sections.0.heading.source: Images have makers, audiences and settings
read.sections.0.heading.back: Images have makers, audiences and settings

read.sections.0.text.source:
Art history studies images and objects together with the people who made, supported, bought, and used them. An artwork's composition, or arrangement, directs attention. Its medium, or material, affects how it was made and how people experience it. Two different works connect artistic choices with work, wealth, and the ways people picture their surroundings.

Katsushika Hokusai made Under the Wave off Kanagawa around 1830–32, during Japan's Edo period. It belongs to a series called Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. Curving water fills the picture, while the mountain appears as a small triangle in the distance. His landscapes used indigo and imported Prussian blue, so an image of a Japanese place also connects with materials that moved across borders.

Edo-period Japan was governed by the Tokugawa military government. Growing cities and trade supported prosperous merchants and craftspeople, often called chōnin, or townspeople. Their spending helped keep a market going for pictures of actors, entertainment, and famous places. Money did not give merchants the highest official social rank. Buyers' interests mattered alongside artists' ideas and government rules. Hokusai worked within this city culture; his prints do not express everything about Japan.
read.sections.0.text.back:
Art history studies images and objects together with the people who made, supported, bought and used them. An artwork's composition, or arrangement, directs attention. The work's medium, or material, affects how the work was made and how people experience it. Two different works connect artists' choices with work, wealth and the way people picture the surroundings around them.

Katsushika Hokusai made Under the Wave off Kanagawa (Under the Wave off the Coast of Kanagawa) around 1830–32, in the Edo period in Japan. This work belongs to a series named Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji). Curving water fills the picture, while the mountain appears as a small triangle in the distance. His landscape pictures used indigo and imported Prussian blue, so a picture of a place in Japan is also connected with materials that moved across national borders.

Japan in the Edo period was governed by the Tokugawa military government. Growing cities and trade supported prosperous merchants and craftspeople, often called chōnin, or townspeople. Their spending helped keep a market for pictures of actors, entertainment and famous places. Money did not give merchants the highest official social position. Buyers' interests helped decide, alongside artists' ideas and government rules. Hokusai worked within this city culture; his prints do not express everything about Japan.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Melintasi batas negara" (across national borders) for "across borders"; Edo Japan had no modern national borders in the same sense, so reviewers may prefer "melintasi batas wilayah".

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Art history looks at objects and the people around them. Who made them? Who paid? Who used them? The composition is how the parts are arranged. It leads your eye. The medium is what a work is made of.

Hokusai made Under the Wave off Kanagawa around 1830 in Japan. Huge waves fill the picture. Mount Fuji is a small shape far away. He used a blue paint that came from Europe. So a picture of Japan also used things from far away.

At that time, military rulers governed Japan. Cities grew. Many traders and craftspeople had money. People called them townspeople. They bought pictures of actors and famous places. But money did not give them the top rank. Hokusai made prints for this city market.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
Art history studies objects and the people around them. Who made it? Who paid? Who used it? Composition is the way the parts of a work are arranged. Composition guides your eye. Medium is the material of a work.

Hokusai made Under the Wave off Kanagawa around 1830 in Japan. Big waves fill the picture. Mount Fuji looks small in the distance. He used a blue paint that came from Europe. So a picture about Japan also used materials from a faraway place.

At that time, military rulers governed Japan. Cities grew. Many merchants and craftspeople had money. People called them townspeople. They bought pictures of actors and famous places. But money did not give them the highest position. Hokusai made prints for this city market.

read.sections.1.heading.source: How a woodblock print was made
read.sections.1.heading.back: How a woodcut print was made

read.sections.1.text.source:
This work is a woodblock print. A design is transferred to a block of wood. Areas are cut away, and the raised surface takes the ink. Paper laid over it takes the image. Colour printing uses separate blocks lined up on the same sheet. Many impressions, or printed copies, can come from the blocks.

Several specialists worked together. The designer supplied the image, a carver prepared the blocks, a printer added the colours, and a publisher ran the business. Publishers helped choose subjects and how carefully a print was made. A famous artist's name identifies one contribution within a wider world of skilled work and business.
read.sections.1.text.back:
This work is a woodcut print. A design is moved onto a block of wood. Certain parts are gouged out, and the raised surface takes the ink. Paper laid on top of it takes the picture. Colour prints use separate blocks printed exactly lined up on the same sheet. Many impressions, or printed copies, can be made from the blocks.

Several experts worked together. The designer supplied the picture, the carver prepared the blocks, the printer added the colours, and the publisher ran the business. Publishers helped choose the subject and how carefully a print was made. A famous artist's name only shows one contribution within a wider world of skilled work and business.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Hasil cetak" (printed result) for "impression", so it is not confused with "cetakan" (print). Glossary word.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
This picture is a woodblock print. A design is put on a block of wood. Some parts are cut away. Ink goes on the raised parts. Paper on top takes the picture. Each colour has its own block. Many copies, called impressions, come from the same blocks.

Many people made one print. An artist drew it. A carver cut the blocks. A printer added the colours. A publisher sold the prints. So a famous name is only one part of the work.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
This picture is a woodcut print. A design is put on a block of wood. Some parts are gouged out. Ink is put on the raised parts. Paper on top takes the picture. Each colour has its own block. Many copies, called impressions, are made from the same blocks.

Many people make one print. An artist draws it. A carver gouges the block. A printer adds the colours. A publisher sells the prints. So a famous name is only one part of the work.

read.sections.2.text.source:
Pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Harvesters is an oil painting on oak from 1565. Workers cut grain and rest beneath a tree. A wealthy merchant in Antwerp ordered its series of seasons for the dining room of his country house. The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes the farm scene as sympathetic, but idealised for that patron.

Here the word Netherlandish describes a historical region, not the Dutch state of today. Antwerp, now in Belgium, belonged to the Low Countries, ruled by the Habsburg family. It was a centre of trade, printing, and art markets. A picture of the countryside could hang in the cultured home of someone whose wealth and daily life were in the city. Knowing this setting stops us from mistaking the patron's chosen view for the life of every farm worker.

A print was made in many copies for many buyers; a commissioned painting served one patron and one room. Both organise attention, but their audiences and ways of making differ. Form and historical context together help explain how each work belonged to a society.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Harvesters (The Harvesters) is an oil painting on oak wood from 1565. Workers cut grain and rest under a tree. A rich merchant in Antwerp ordered this series of seasons for the dining room of his house in the countryside. The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes the farm scene as full of sympathy, but made more beautiful than reality for that patron.

Here, the word Netherlandish (from the Low Countries) points to a region in history, not the Dutch state of today. Antwerp, which is now in Belgium, belonged to the Low Countries, which were ruled by the Habsburg family. The city was a centre of trade, printing and art markets. A painting of the countryside could hang in the cultured home of someone whose wealth and daily life were in the city. Knowing this setting stops us from mistaking the patron's chosen view for the life of every farm worker.

A print was made in many copies for many buyers; a commissioned painting served one patron and one room. Both organise attention, but their audiences and ways of making differ. Form and historical context together help explain how each work became part of a society.
read.sections.2.text.note: The English keeps the word "Netherlandish", which the museum uses for Bruegel; it is kept, glossed. "Antwerpen" is the usual Indonesian spelling. "Patron" is used in Indonesian art writing; reviewers may prefer "pemesan" or "penyokong".

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Bruegel painted The Harvesters in 1565 on a wooden panel. Workers cut grain and rest under a tree. A rich trader in the city of Antwerp was its patron. He paid for it. It hung in the dining room of his country house. The museum says the scene is kind to the workers. But it is nicer than real life.

Antwerp is now in Belgium. Then it was a busy city of trade and art. So this picture of farm work hung in a rich city home. It shows his view, not the life of every worker.

A print was made in many copies for many buyers. A painting was made for one person and one room. Looking at the work and its context together helps us understand it.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Bruegel painted The Harvesters in 1565 on a wooden panel. Workers cut grain and rest under a tree. A rich merchant in the city of Antwerp was the patron of the painting. He paid for the painting. The painting hung in the dining room of his house in the country. The museum says the painting looks at the workers kindly. But the painting is more beautiful than real life.

Now Antwerp is in Belgium. Then the city was busy with trade and art. So this painting of farm work hung in the home of a rich person from the city. The painting shows his view, not the life of every worker.

Prints were made in many copies for many buyers. A painting was made for one person and one room. Looking at the work and its historical context together helps us understand it.

write.prompt.back: Pick Hokusai's print or Bruegel's painting. Explain how one thing you can see and one fact from its history help you understand the work. Two or three sentences are enough.

write.sentenceStarters.0.source: In the picture, I can see ...
write.sentenceStarters.0.back: In the picture, I can see ...

write.example.source: In Hokusai's print, I can see a huge wave in front and Mount Fuji very small behind it. The history tells us that prints like this were made in many copies and sold to townspeople in Japan's growing cities. Together, these show that the picture was made to catch the eye of buyers. It does not show everything about life in Japan.
write.example.back: In Hokusai's print, I can see a big wave in front and Mount Fuji very small behind it. Its history tells us that prints like this were made in many copies and sold to townspeople in Japan's growing cities. Together, these things show that the picture was made to catch buyers' attention. The picture does not show everything about life in Japan.
